facts.fact: Green water is a bloom of tiny free-floating algae (phytoplankton) that stay suspended in the water and turn it cloudy green, sometimes called 'pea soup'.
Green water is caused by single-celled phytoplankton that multiply very quickly.
Green water is not directly harmful to fish or shrimp.
Green water can be food for fry and invertebrates, and some breeders grow it on purpose.
Green water is useful for raising baby fish, but it hides the view and can block light from plants.
At night the algae use up oxygen, so a heavy bloom combined with weak aeration can stress or kill fish and shrimp.
Algae make oxygen by day but use oxygen at night, and a dense bloom can drive dissolved oxygen close to zero overnight.
When a large bloom dies back, bacteria break down the dead algae and oxygen production stops, which can cause oxygen depletion and fish kills.
The water itself looks cloudy green (the algae float in the water rather than growing on glass or decor).
After an algae die-off the water usually changes from deep green to black, gray, brown or clear.
With low oxygen, fish hang at the surface in the early morning. In severe cases they gulp air and ignore disturbances.
Too much light causes green water, especially direct sunlight on the tank.
Excess nutrients, for example accidentally double-dosing fertilizer, can trigger green water.
An ammonia spike can trigger green water. It may come from a new, uncycled tank or from overfeeding, for example by a pet sitter.
Other causes are sunlight from a window, leaving lights on too long, overfeeding, overstocking, liquid fertilizer, and infrequent maintenance that lets waste and nitrate build up.
Keep aeration and equipment running and watch the fish for oxygen stress, since the algae use oxygen at night.
Running out of trace minerals or nutrients is probably the most common reason a large bloom dies back, and the die-off can then deplete oxygen.
Blackout: cover the tank completely for at least a week. It works, but it is hard on plants.
Blackout: turn the lights off, keep equipment running, and cover the tank fully for no more than 7 days. Move livestock to a temporary tank if possible.
After a blackout, do a large water change, because the dying algae can spike ammonia.
A UV sterilizer kills green-water algae, typically within two to three days.
In a UV sterilizer, water flows slowly past a UV bulb that damages the DNA of the algae so they cannot reproduce. Regular water changes then clear the water.
Green water is fairly easy to treat with UV, so a small sterilizer is usually enough.
UV sterilizers barely affect beneficial bacteria, because those bacteria live mostly on the filter and on surfaces rather than floating in the water.
Fine filter floss, polishing pads or filter socks can trap the small suspended particles.
UV also causes algae die-off, so watch for an ammonia spike.
Step 1: find and cut the cause (shorten the light period, move the tank out of sunlight, feed less, check nitrate and phosphate).
Step 2: clear the water with a blackout of up to 7 days or with a UV sterilizer, while keeping the filter and aeration running.
Step 3: do a large water change after the treatment to remove dead algae and ammonia.
Step 4: keep up weekly water changes of at least 20%. Combined methods may take a couple of weeks to show results.
Keep the aquarium light on for no more than 6–8 hours a day, and use a dimmer if the light is strong.
Add fast-growing plants that compete with the algae for nutrients and light, such as Salvinia natans, water sprite (Ceratopteris siliquosa), hornwort, and other stem or floating plants.
Replace at least 20% of the water weekly, and clean a correctly sized filter every 1–2 months.
Avoid overfeeding and overstocking, and test regularly for nitrate and phosphate.
Relying on large water changes alone does not work, because the algae reproduce rapidly.
Dosing liquid fertilizer into a tank that already gets too much light is a mistake.
Running a blackout without moving the livestock or preparing for an ammonia spike is a mistake.
Buce Plant says the idea that a big water change cures green water is wrong, because the algae regrow quickly.
Vietnamese names include 'tảo xanh' (green algae) and 'nước hồ xanh đục' (murky green water).
Vietnamese names include 'tảo phù du' (phytoplankton), 'tảo nở hoa' (algae bloom) and 'nước xanh rêu' (moss-green water).
Vietnamese shops sell UV lamps ('đèn UV') and air pumps ('máy sủi oxy') for green water, and link green water to strong sun on uncovered outdoor and koi ponds.
Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, which makes night-time oxygen loss from a dense bloom more dangerous (relevant to Vietnam's hot season).
